list.listitem: Suspect mixed connective tissue disorder (MCTD) in any patient, particularly a young woman, who presents with Raynaud's phenomenon and features of other connective tissue diseases. C
High-titer antiribonucleoprotein (also known as U1-RNP, RNP, and nuclear RNP or nRNP) autoantibodies are required for diagnosis. C
Clinical course is variable, ranging from spontaneous remission to progressive organ dysfunction and poor response to therapy. B
Pulmonary hypertension and infection are the most frequent causes of mortality and should be aggressively sought. B

Therapy should be tailored to the severity of the disease manifestations, and may include conventional therapies used for similar conditions not associated with MCTD, in addition to immunosuppression when necessary. C

background.definition: MCTD is a distinct clinical entity characterized by overlapping features of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), scleroderma, myositis, and rheumatoid arthritis in the setting of a high titer of autoantibodies to a defined nuclear antigen, known as U1-ribonucleoprotein (U1-RNP, also called RNP or nRNP).

list.listitem: A Norwegian study estimated an incidence of 2.1/million adults/year and a point prevalence of 3.8 per 100,000 adults. The same study found a ratio of women to men of 3.3 to 1, and a mean age of onset of 38 years.
The annual incidence of MCTD in 1985 to 2014 in Olmsted County, Minnesota, was 1.9 per 100,000 population; 50 cases were identified with a mean age of 48.1 years, 84% were female.
MCTD is thought to be more common than dermatomyositis (1-2 cases per 100,000 population), less common than SLE (15-50 cases per 100,000), and about as common as systemic sclerosis.
There is no apparent racial or ethnic predisposition for this condition.
In a US American Indian/Alaska Native 2007 database, age-adjusted prevalence of MCTD by rheumatologist diagnosis was 6.4 per 100,000 (95% confidence interval (CI) 2.8-12.8).
Fundamental cause of MCTD remains uncertain.
Loss of T and B cell tolerance, possibly initiated by an environmental trigger acting in a genetically-predisposed individual appears central to disease initiation.
Interleukin-10 gene variants appear to be genetic risk factors for MCTD susceptibility.

In addition, human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B*08 (odds ratio [OR] 2.05) and DRB1*04:01 (OR 2.82) have been identified as risk alleles for MCTD; B*18 and DRB1 were independent risk factors for pulmonary fibrosis.
Self-antigens, including the characteristic U1-70 kDa molecule, are exposed to the immune system, due to molecular mimicry either by infectious agents or by abnormalities of apoptosis.
Antigen-presenting cells present autoantigen associated with specific human leukocyte antigen molecules to T cells.
T cell dysfunction occurs, with anti-U1-70 kDa autoreactive T cells present in circulating blood.
Autoreactive T cells produce cytokines, which expand the autoreactive T cell clone and promote proliferation and differentiation of the autoantigen-presenting cells.
Exposure to these pro-inflammatory factors leads to premature atherosclerosis.
B cells may function as antigen-presenting cells after the binding of an autoantigen to surface immunoglobulins.

Autoreactive B and T cells then act in concert via a final common pathway that results in high-titer anti-U1-RNP antibodies and vascular endothelial proliferation, with widespread lymphocytic infiltration of tissues and organ dysfunction.

Diagnosis of MCTD requires positive high-titer anti-U1-RNP autoantibody and at least three of the following clinical features: swollen hands, Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, myositis, and arthritis. One of these criteria must be either arthritis or myositis. C
Positive results for anti-Smith, anti-double-stranded DNA are not seen, and should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis such as SLE. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Anti-Smith (Sm) and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies more typical serological profile
Prominent muscle involvement, without coexisting features of scleroderma: Raynaud's phenomenon uncommon
Typical serological picture includes anti-Scl or anticentromere antibodies; muscle and joint involvement less prominent

A spectrum of disorders, including MCTD, results in elevated pulmonary arterial pressure; nonspecific symptoms such as dyspnea, fatigue, digital ulceration and sclerodactyly; pulmonary function testing helpful and right-heart catheterization confirms diagnosis
No evidence of autoantibody production or other features of connective tissue disease
Characteristic rash, lymphadenopathy; no high-titer autoantibodies; positive HIV RNA
Muscle and skin involvement unusual; joint erosions seen on x-rays; more aggressive joint damage

list.listitem: MCTD should be considered in any patient, particularly a young woman, who presents with Raynaud's phenomenon and any of the following: arthralgias/arthritis, swollen hands, symptoms of esophageal dysmotility, or dyspnea.
Raynaud's phenomenon is the most common finding.
In the 50 incident cases identified in Olmstead county, Raynaud's phenomenon was found in half, followed by arthralgia (30%) and swollen hands (16%).

A review of case reports and case series of MCTD in children (215 children, 82% female), the mean age at diagnosis was 11.8 years. The most common symptoms at presentation were Raynaud's phenomenon (70%), muscular involvement (54%, skin signs, 40%, swollen hands or fingers (29%), join pains (26%) and fever (22%). Less common were lymphadenopathy (11%), serositis (10%), xeroftalmia (4%), xerostomia (4%) and ocular involvement (1%).

Physical examination may confirm other features of overlapping connective tissue syndromes, including synovitis, skin thickening and tightening, malar or heliotrope rash, pleural or pericardial effusion, and evidence of increased pulmonary pressures.
A Japanese study found that SLE-like symptoms are more common in patients with juvenile-onset MCTD than in adults; scleroderma-like features were less common.
Cardiac involvement is seen in 13% to 65% of patients, based on reports from 11 case series. Abnormalities include pericarditis (30%-43%), diastolic dysfunction, and accelerated atherosclerosis.

Secondary Sjögren's syndrome was found in 14/44 consecutive patients with MCTD. The diagnosis was based on the American-European Consensus Group criteria: ocular and oral symptoms plus 2 of: ocular signs, salivary gland involvement or histopathology, or antibodies to Ro(SSA) or La(SSB) antigens.
CBC: Leukopenia and anemia occur in 50% to 75% of patients. Anemia is usually consistent with chronic disease; autoimmune hemolysis is rare and thrombocytopenia is relatively uncommon.
Routine blood chemistry provides evaluation of renal function. Proteinuria, hematuria, or casts occur in those uncommon patients with glomerulonephritis.

A high-titer speckled pattern of antinuclear antibodies is typical but not specific for MCTD. Anti-U1-RNP antibodies are essential for the diagnosis of MCTD, and the anti-U1-70 kDa antibody is characteristic of the disease. Anti-Smith (Sm) and anti-double-stranded antibodies are typical of SLE and not seen in MCTD. Anticentromere and antitopoisomerase (or anti-Scl 70) antibodies are typical of the scleroderma spectrum of diseases and are absent in MCTD. Anti-endothelial cell antibodies also appear to be common in this disorder.
Rheumatoid factor is detected in over 50% of patients.

Antiphospholipid antibodies are uncommon (approximately 15%) and do not appear to confer increased risk of thrombotic events or pregnancy complications, although they may be markers of pulmonary hypertension.
CXR may demonstrate infiltrates, effusions, or cardiomegaly in those with lung involvement.

Pulmonary function tests, including diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO), are useful to monitor for the development of pulmonary hypertension. Falling DLCO may be the first indication of elevated pulmonary pressures. Echocardiography is used to assess ejection fraction and provide initial screening for pulmonary hypertension. Right heart catheterization is the most accurate test to evaluate suspected pulmonary hypertension and to assess for responsiveness to vasodilator therapy.
American College of Rheumatology guidelines (2024) recommend screening patients with MCTD for interstital lung disease with PFTs and high resolution computed tomography.
First described as a condition with overlapping features of SLE, scleroderma, and polymyositis. Patients with MCTD do not have all the features of these conditions.

Diagnostic criteria of Alarcon-Segovia and Villarreal are as follows: serological evidence of positive anti-U1-RNP, with a passive hemagglutination titer of at least 1:1600 must be demonstrated and at least 3 of the following clinical criteria: edema of the hands, Raynaud's phenomenon, acrosclerosis (progressive systemic sclerosis), myositis, or synovitis. Either myositis or synovitis must be present to meet criteria.
Treatment should be tailored to the organ system involved and the severity of the organ's involvement. C
NSAIDs, hydroxychloroquine, and low-dose steroids are the mainstays for non-organ-threatening symptoms. C
Higher doses of corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents may be necessary for more severe organ involvement. C

Conventional therapies for conditions such as pulmonary hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux, and Raynaud's phenomenon have been successfully used in patients with MCTD, although RCTs specifically in patients with MCTD are lacking. C
Drug therapy should be tailored to the severity of disease manifestations and the organ systems involved. Fatigue, arthralgias, and myalgias usually respond to NSAIDs or hydroxychloroquine.

No trials have evaluated the efficacy of therapies for Raynaud's phenomenon associated with MCTD. A Cochrane meta-analysis of calcium channel blockers for Raynaud's phenomenon in general found 38 RCTs with 982 participants (most were crossover studies, hence the small sample size). Studies included both patients with primary and secondary Raynaud's. They found a reduction of 6 attacks per week from approximately 14 with placebo. However, this was driven by an outlier that found a very large reduction; removing it attenuated the benefit to 3 fewer attacks per week. Attack severity was also decreased, but it is unclear whether the effect was clinically important. They also concluded that high doses appear to be more effective, but also that the drug appears more effective for primary than secondary Raynaud's.
Arthralgias/arthritis can be treated with NSAIDs and antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine; low-dose corticosteroids or methotrexate can be added in more severe cases.
Serositis, leukopenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia can usually be managed with low to moderate doses of corticosteroids.

Esophageal dysmotility with gastroesophageal reflux disease symptoms responds to proton pump inhibitors. A case series of 10 patients with progressive systemic sclerosis or MCTD found no effect of a single intravenous dose of cisapride, a gastroprokinetic agent, on esophageal motor function.

Trials have evaluated vasodilators such as epoprostenol, treprostinil, endothelin antagonists such as bosentan, and the phosphodiesterase inhibitor sildenafil (20-80 mg orally three times daily) for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension; some of these patients had scleroderma or SLE. The studies found evidence for benefit in improving symptoms, exercise capacity, and cardiopulmonary hemodynamics.
Randomized trials specifically in patients with MCTD-associated pulmonary hypertension are not available. Immunosuppression with steroids and cyclophosphamide has been successful in case reports.

For adult patients with severe progressive interstitial lung disease associated with CTD, investigators in a phase 2 RCT comparing rituximab (1000 mg at weeks 0 and 2 intravenously) with cyclophosphamide (600 mg/m2body surface area every 4 weeks intravenously for six doses) in 101 patients, found both drugs improved FVC from baseline at 24 weeks and improved respiratory-related quality-of-life measures at 48 weeks. Serious adverse events occurred in 33 patients in the cyclophosphamide group and 29 in the rituximab group, with 2/48 patients (4%) receiving cyclophosphamide and 3/49 (6%) receiving rituximab dying of disease-related complications during the study
Diet and activity appropriate for promotion of cardiovascular health are important to this population predisposed to atherosclerotic heart disease.
Patients should be educated on lifestyle modifications such as cold avoidance to reduce Raynauds and dietary changes to reduce reflux symptoms.
Cold avoidance should be recommended to all patients with Raynaud's phenomenon.
Patients with MCTD should be co-managed by a rheumatologist experienced in their care.
Referral to a cardiologist and pulmonologist is essential for optimal management of pulmonary hypertension.

As with other rheumatologic conditions, patients are at elevated risk of cardiovascular events. EULAR guidelines (2022) recommend cardiovascular risk assessments using standard tools. Blood pressure and lipid management should follow standard general population guidance. Use of low dose aspirin is not recommended, a change from earlier guidelines.

Interstitial lung disease with pulmonary fibrosis is a relatively common complication of MCTD. Evidence can be found in half of patients after 10 years, with severe disease in 20%. In severe cases transplant has been performed in these patients.
"Drop Head Syndrome," weakness of the neck extensors leading to inability to hold the head upright, has been reported as a rare complication. It responded to prednisolone in one case report.
Dysphagia has been reported, and appeared to respond to IV immunoglobulin in one case report.
Thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura (TTP) has been reported in patients with MCTD, with a high case fatality rate. In one case report, it was successfully treated with therapeutic plasma exchange.
Three prospective studies found an overall mortality of 10.4% over 13 to 15 years; cardiac disease was a common cause. B
After 8 years, 58% still had MCTD while 17% had evolved into systemic sclerosis, 9% into SLE, 3% into rheumatoid arthritis, and 11% were no longer affected. B

Only a few, small long-term prospective studies are available. An Italian series of 161 patients with MCTD found that after 8 years, 58% still had MCTD, 17% evolved into systemic sclerosis, 9% into SLE, 3% into rheumatoid arthritis, and 11% were no longer affected.
Three prospective studies found an overall mortality of 10.4% over 13 to 15 years; almost one quarter (20%) of the mortality was attributable to cardiac disease.

In the Olmstead County cohort of 50 patients, after 10 years, evolution to other connective tissue diseases occurred infrequently at 8.5% for SLE and 6.3% for systemic sclerosis. In this cohort, mortality rate was not different from the general population.

Raynaud's phenomenon and esophageal hypomotility generally improve over time. Renal involvement is less common than in SLE and more responsive to treatment. Severe CNS manifestations are rare. Inflammatory manifestations such as skin rashes, serositis, and synovitis generally respond well to corticosteroid therapy. Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, digital ulcers, and pulmonary hypertension are less responsive to immunosuppression.

About one-third of patients will have a benign course and go into remission, one-third will have disease that requires ongoing immunosuppressive treatment even after many years, and one-third will have an aggressive course and poorer response to therapy. The presence of anti-survival motor neuron complex antibodies is a poor prognostic indicator.

In a cohort of 126 patients with MCTD for a mean duration of 9 years, half had abnormal findings on high resolution CT. Lung fibrosis was the most common abnormal finding, which was severe in 19%. Severe lung fibrosis was associated with much higher mortality after a mean of 4.2 years follow-up (20.8% vs. 3.3% in patients with a normal high resolution CT.
In one retrospective cohort study of 39 patients wih MCTD, 51% had abnormal PFTs at baseline but these abnormalities were mild and progressed only slightly after 10 years.
A case control study of 50 patients with juvenile-onset MCTD found a 4-fold increase in the risk of left ventricular dysfunction a median of 15 years later.
A systematic review of 8 studies with 983 patients found a prevalence of pulmonary arterial hypertension of 12.5% in patients with MCTD.

Data from the Registry to Evaluate Early and Long-Term Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Disease Management (REVEAL) demonstrates 1-, 3-, 5-, and 7-year survival rates from time of diagnosis of pulmonary artery hypertension by right-sided heart catheterization of 85%, 68%, 57%, and 49%, respectively.

Consider monitoring for pulmonary hypertension with pulmonary function testing, including DLCO every 6 to 12 months; early detection may allow for better response to treatment, although no trials are available to support this recommendation.
Pregnancy outcome is uncertain, with some studies reporting excellent maternal and fetal outcomes and others suggesting decreased parity and increased risk of miscarriage.

Authors of a systematic review identified 68 cases and added 12 from their institution; about one third had active disease (37.1%). Maternal complications included preeclampsia (N = 13), thromboembolism events, and death (N = 2 for each). Fetal complications included prematurity (48.1%, N = 25), intrauterine growth restriction (38.3%, N = 19), and neonatal lupus (28.6%, N = 18). The perinatal mortality rate was 17.7% (N = 14). Women with active disease had higher rates of prematurity (OR 7.60, 95% CI 1.93-29.95) and perinatal death (OR 16.83, 95% CI 1.90 to 147.70).
Corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine are the mainstays of treatment during pregnancy.
Pregnancies in patients with MCTD should be co-managed by a rheumatologist with experience in this disease and an obstetrician with expertise in high-risk pregnancies.

In a cohort study of 55 patients with juvenile-onset MCTD in Norway, after a mean disease duration of 16.2 years, 52 had continued MCTD (67% with active disease associated with higher anti-ribonucleoprotein antibody levels and positive RF) and 3 developed SLE. The most common disease manifestations were Raynaud's phenomenon (100%), arthritis (94%), puffy hands (77%) and pulmonary manifestations (58%). Most (65%) had evidence of organ damage.
